inline.s: If I attain Buddhahood, and sentient beings of the ten directions, who wish to be reborn in my land, call upon my name even as few as ten times, and yet are not reborn through the power of my vow, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.”
(from the Contemplation of the Dharma-gate)
If I attain Buddhahood, and sentient beings of the ten directions call upon my name even as few as ten times, and yet are not reborn, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.”
from the Praise of Rebirth)
The “as few as ten thoughts” and “as few as ten voices” spoken of here, taken together with what Master Shandao instructed above —
“Precisely because recitation of the name is easy, unbroken thought brings rebirth. If one can
continue thought after thought to the end of life
, then of ten, ten are reborn, and of a hundred, a hundred are reborn”
—make it clear that this is an abbreviated way of saying “for a whole life span, thought after thought continuing, and at the very least,
the ten unbroken thoughts at the moment of death
,” for Master Shandao has already said plainly:
“Thought after thought continuing, to the end of life.”
And
“Thought after thought continuing, to the end of life”
is precisely in order to make thought-after-thought continuing a firmly formed habit,
so as to ensure the ten unbroken thoughts at the moment of death
If, at the moment of death, one does not recitate, or recitates with a scattered mind, then one has not fulfilled
“thought after thought continuing, to the end of life”
Therefore,
“down to ten thoughts, and if not reborn, may I not attain perfect enlightenment”
means precisely this:
the ten unbroken thoughts at the moment of death bring immediate rebirth.
[Ten thoughts, ten voices] Reciting the Buddha’s name for ten thought-moments.
[Thought after thought continuing, formed into a habit] Through constant repeated practice, making thought-after-thought continuing a natural instinct.
Note:
The “down to ten thoughts (ten voices)” taught by Master Shandao is without any doubt the ten thoughts of continuous recitation at the moment of death, for this is
right mindfulness at the moment of death

. Yet in recent years, through the inroads of the Primal Vow teaching, right and wrong have become confounded, and two other interpretations have appeared: first, that “down to ten thoughts (ten voices)” means having recited the Buddha’s name at least ten times, so that anyone who has ever recited it ten times in daily life will certainly be reborn — this is the theoretical basis for “recitation of the name necessarily brings rebirth”; second, that “down to ten thoughts (ten voices)” means ten thoughts of scattered-mind recitation at the moment of death — this is the theoretical basis for the claim that scattered-mind recitation also brings certain rebirth. Both interpretations are erroneous. For
if
one has
merely recited the Buddha’s name ten times in daily life but
does not recitate at the moment of death, or, though recitating, recitates with a scattered mind, neither case fulfills
“thought after thought continuing, to the end of life”
Therefore
“down to ten thoughts (ten voices)”
means at the very least
the ten thoughts of continuous recitation at the moment of death
. Hence Master Daochuo instructed clearly:
If there be sentient beings who, even having committed evil all their lives, at the moment of death
recite for ten thoughts without break
, calling upon my name,
and are not reborn, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.”
(from the Collected Essays on the Peaceful Grove)

blocks.text: 3. Right Mindfulness at the Moment of Death

inline.s: Whether rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss requires right mindfulness at the moment of death
is the watershed that divides the orthodox teaching of the Pure Land school from heretical views
. Orthodox teaching follows the scriptures and affirms that right mindfulness at death is required; hence Master Shandao instructed:
“Unbroken thought brings rebirth.”
Master Yongming instructed:
“The ten thoughts at the moment of death are accomplished.”
Master Lianchi instructed:
“Within, right mindfulness gathers; without, the Buddha comes to welcome.”
Master Yinguang instructed:

“All who recitate the Buddha’s name should give rise to the great bodhi-mind of universally saving sentient beings; then the circumstances of this present life will be smooth, and with right mindfulness at death they will be reborn. From this they depart from the stream of ordinary beings and join the ranks of sages and worthies; relying on the Buddha’s compassionate power and their own vow, they turn back into the Saha world, manifesting all manner of forms to liberate sentient beings.”
The patriarchs of the Pure Land school have likewise taught again and again:
rebirth through right mindfulness at the moment of death.
(See further
“Right Mindfulness at Death”
, in the article)

But the heretical doctrine of the Primal Vow teaching violates the scriptures and denies the need for right mindfulness at death, proclaiming that recitation of the name necessarily brings rebirth, that one need not observe precepts, need not cultivate merit, need not purify one’s own mind — and that even committing evil throughout one’s life is of no consequence.
[Purify one’s own mind] From the admonition-verse shared by the seven Buddhas:
“Refrain from all evil, practice all good, purify your own mind — this is the teaching of all Buddhas.”

The seven Buddhas of the past all took this verse as the principle of their precept practice, so it is called the “admonition-verse shared by the seven Buddhas.” The heretical doctrine of the Primal Vow teaching urges that “one need not observe precepts,” which is to deny “refrain from all evil”; “one need not cultivate merit,” which is to deny “practice all good”; and furthermore one need not “purify one’s own mind.” Can this still be called Buddhism? [Seven Buddhas] The seven Buddhas of the past, namely Vipasyin, Sikhin, Visvabhu, Krakucchanda, Kanakamuni, Kasyapa, and Sakyamuni Buddha.
Moreover, in the Commentary in Four Fascicles on the Contemplation Sutra, Master Shandao explained the meaning of the section on “the lowest grade, the lowest birth”:

“From ‘such a foolish person’ down to ‘the offense of birth-and-death,’ it clearly sets forth the benefits gained in this very life through hearing the Dharma and reciting the Buddha’s name; there are ten points: first, it again identifies the person who has committed evil; second, it shows that his life has little time remaining; third, it shows that at death he meets a good spiritual friend; fourth, it shows that the good person comforts and instructs him to recitate the Buddha’s name; fifth, it shows that the pains of death press upon the offender so that he cannot of himself recite the name; sixth, it shows that the good friend, knowing his suffering and lost mindfulness, turns to teach him to call aloud the name of Amitabha; seventh, it shows how many recitations there are, voice after voice without interruption; eighth, it shows the removal of offenses of many kalpas; ninth, it shows that
with right mindfulness at death
, a golden lotus forthwith arrives to respond; tenth, it shows the swiftness or slowness of departure, until he reaches the land of his destination.”
Please note especially that here Master Shandao says:
rebirth through right mindfulness at death
(“with right mindfulness at death, a golden lotus forthwith arrives to respond”). (See further
“Commentary on the Lowest Grade, Lowest Birth Section of the Contemplation Sutra”
, in the article.) Yet the Primal Vow teaching, which loudly claims to “rely upon Master Shandao,” firmly opposes rebirth through right mindfulness at death
— is this, then, how one relies upon him?!
For more on right mindfulness at death, please refer to
“Right Mindfulness at Death”
and
“Right Mindfulness at Death: Answers to a Guest’s Questions”
, in these two articles.
The following instruction is taken from Master Shandao’s Essay on Right Mindfulness and Rebirth at Death (see further
“Master Shandao’s Essay on Right Mindfulness and Rebirth at Death (Annotated)”
[If, at the approach of the end of a grave illness, the relatives must not shed tears and weep, nor raise sounds of sighing and regret, which would disturb the patient’s mind and
cause him to lose right mindfulness

. Let them recite the Buddha’s name together with one voice; only when the breath has ceased may they weep. If there is the least attachment to this world in his heart, it becomes an obstruction, and he cannot be liberated. If there is someone who understands the Pure Land, and comes often to encourage him, that is a great fortune. If one does according to this, he will certainly be reborn beyond, without doubt.]

If, when a grave illness approaches the end of life, the relatives must not shed tears and weep, nor raise sounds of sighing and regret, lest they disturb the patient’s mind and spirit and make him lose right mindfulness. They must recite the Buddha’s name with one voice, and only after the patient’s breath has ceased may they weep. For if the patient has the least attachment to this world, it becomes an obstruction to rebirth, and he cannot be liberated. If there is someone who understands the Pure Land and comes often to encourage him, this is most fortunate. If one acts according to this, the patient will certainly and without doubt be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss.

This method — practiced by monks, laypeople, and those who have never recitated, — all are reborn, without any doubt. I have seen many in the world who, in ordinary daily life, recitate the Buddha’s name, praise and bow, and make vows to be reborn in the West, with great
earnestness and sincerity

. Yet when they come to be ill, they are afraid of death, and speak no more of rebirth and liberation. Only when their breath has faded and life has ended, and their consciousness has entered the dark realm, do they at last begin to recitate and strike the bell. This is exactly like closing the door after the thief has gone — of what use is it? Birth and death are a great matter;
one must exert one’s own strength
to succeed.
If there be a single thought-moment of error
(if the final thought at death is a deluded thought rather than right mindfulness)
, and one suffers for many kalpas
, who can take your place?
Think on this! Think on this!
When one is free of illness, one should earnestly take up and hold this method — this is the great matter of the final hour.]

This “method of right mindfulness and rebirth at death” (the patient must do his utmost to maintain right mindfulness at death; the relatives must not weep or lament lest they disturb the patient’s right mindfulness; and a good spiritual friend’s timely guidance and encouragement can help the patient arouse and sustain right mindfulness at death) — practiced by monks, laypeople, and those who have never recitated, — all are reborn, with no doubt whatever. I have seen many in the world who, in ordinary daily life, recitate the Buddha’s name, praise and bow, and vow to be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss, most earnestly and sincerely. Yet when illness comes, they are afraid of death and speak no more of rebirth and liberation. Only when their own breath has faded and life ended, and their consciousness has been cast into the dark realm, do they at last recitate and strike the bell. This is exactly like closing the door after the thief has gone (it is too late to shut the door against theft after the thief has already taken the goods) — of what use is it? Birth and death are a great matter;
one must diligently apply one’s own effort
to succeed.
If the final thought at death be one thought in error
(if the thought at death be a deluded thought rather than right mindfulness)
, the consequence is suffering for many kalpas
, who can take your place?
You must weigh this well! Weigh it well!

Before sickness comes, one should earnestly take up and hold this “method of right mindfulness and rebirth at death” (one should make full preparation for right mindfulness at death in advance — that is what Master Yongming calls “preparing the ferry and the bridge” — and at the same time instruct the relatives that they must not weep or lament; having a good spiritual friend’s help at the final hour is even better). This is the great matter of the final hour!

Question: The Primal Vow teaching claims that “the gate of the Grand Vow,” “recitation of the name necessarily brings rebirth,” and “the evil person as the proper object [of salvation]” are the Pure Land thought of Master Shandao. Is this so?
Answer: This is a complete distortion and slander of Master Shandao’s Pure Land thought! The gate of the Grand Vow was fabricated by Master Honen — see further
“Master Honen’s Fabrication of the Gate of the Grand Vow”
, in that article
. “Recitation of the name necessarily brings rebirth” was likewise fabricated by Master Honen, Master Huijing, Master Jingzong, and others! (See further
“Does Recitation of the Name Necessarily Bring Rebirth?”
, in that article.) Master Shandao never said “recitation of the name necessarily brings rebirth.” On the contrary, Master Shandao said:
“Unbroken thought brings rebirth”
and “rebirth through right mindfulness at death”

. As for the slander that Master Shandao taught “the evil person as the proper object [of salvation],” one has only to look at what Master Shandao instructed in the Commentary in Four Fascicles on the Contemplation Sutra to know the truth of the matter. Master Shandao said:
“Sincere means genuine; truthful means real. To make clear that the understanding and practice cultivated by the body, speech, and mind karma of all sentient beings
must be done from a mind that is truly real
one must not outwardly display the appearance of virtue and diligence while inwardly harboring falsity
, greed, anger, perversity, and deceit, with a hundred kinds of treachery — a nature so vicious that it is hard to be transformed, like serpents and scorpions. Though they produce the three karmas
(of body, speech, and mind)

, this is called “the virtue mixed with poison,” also called “false practice,” and is not real karma. If one settles the mind and practices in this way, though he torment his body and mind, day and night through all twelve periods, rushing and toiling as if his head were on fire, this is all
(a general term for ‘altogether’)
called “the virtue mixed with poison.”
He who wishes to turn this practice mixed with poison around and seek rebirth in the Buddha’s Pure Land
can surely not attain it.”
Master Shandao points out that these evil persons inwardly harboring falsity (and persons such as Honen belong to this class)
“seek rebirth in the Buddha’s Pure Land — this surely cannot be attained”
how can it be said that the salvation of Amitabha takes the evil person as its proper object? (For the refutation of “the evil person as the proper object,” see further
“The Primal Vow Teaching Is an Outwardly-Buddhist Heresy”
, in that article.)

The Buddha-recitation practice has four methods of recitation: first, recitation of the name — single-mindedly calling upon the Buddha’s name; second, recitation before an image — contemplating the Buddha’s image while calling his name; third, recitation by visualization — single-mindedly contemplating the auspicious marks and adornments of the Buddha; fourth, recitation of true reality — single-mindedly contemplating the real Dharmakaya of the Buddha. Among these four methods, which best accords with the capacities of sentient beings, with great merit and easy practice, with little effort and swift effect? Master Shandao, the manifestation of Amitabha Buddha, made a clear decision for us and chose the method most suited to the capacity of the Dharma-ending age — recitation of the name. In the Practice of Specialized and Miscellaneous Cultivation, Master Shandao instructed:

“Sentient beings have heavy obstructions; the realm is subtle while the mind is coarse, consciousness floats and the spirit flies — so visual contemplation is hard to accomplish. Therefore the Great Sage
(Sakyamuni Buddha)
in compassion
directly urged
exclusive recitation of the name
Precisely because recitation of the name is easy,
unbroken thought brings rebirth

(Translation: sentient beings have heavy karmic obstructions; the realm (the object contemplated) is subtle while the mind is coarse, consciousness floats and the spirit flies, so visual-contemplation recitation is hard to accomplish. Therefore Sakyamuni Buddha, in compassion, directly taught them the recitation of the name — to call exclusively upon the name of Amitabha Buddha. Precisely because recitation of the name is easier than visualization, at the moment of death, one need only keep the mindful thought unbroken, and he will be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss.)
Once the great direction is set — that the cultivation of the Pure Land school should devote itself to recitation of the name (
“exclusively call upon the name; unbroken thought brings rebirth”
) — the question that immediately follows is: how are we to ensure
that the mindful thought is unbroken at the moment of death
? Therefore Master Shandao went on to instruct:
“If one can
continue thought after thought to the end of life
one who
(a person who practices thus his whole life)
, then of ten, ten are reborn, and of a hundred, a hundred are reborn......May all people reflect well within themselves: whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, one must
rouse the mind, restrain oneself, day and night never ceasing
; when the final thought ends life, the next thought forthwith brings rebirth; forever enjoying unconditioned Dharma-bliss, and on to Buddhahood — how joyful!”

[Thought after thought continuing, to the end of life] Because, at the moment of death, unbroken mindful thought brings immediate rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss, one should thus practice for one’s whole life, making thought-after-thought continuing a firmly formed habit. Then one will certainly be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss — of ten, ten are reborn; of a hundred, a hundred are reborn.
In this instruction, Master Shandao teaches:
“Exclusively call upon the name; unbroken thought brings rebirth.”
And,
in order to accomplish unbroken thought bringing rebirth at the moment of death, one must
“continue thought after thought to the end of life; rouse the mind, restrain oneself, day and night never ceasing”
, making thought-after-thought continuing a firmly formed habit. Thus the program of practice of the Pure Land school is established:
call exclusively upon the name; unbroken thought brings rebirth; continue thought after thought to the end of life; rouse the mind and restrain oneself, day and night never ceasing.

This thoroughly and completely resolves the fundamental issue of Pure Land practice: which method of recitation to adopt? How to recitate? — in order to ensure rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss!

The “exclusive recitation of the name” of which Master Shandao speaks here is the exclusive recitation of the name that continues thought after thought — that is, what he earlier taught as “single-mindedly invoking the name of Amitabha Buddha,” namely single-minded recitation of the name. Hence “call exclusively upon the name; unbroken thought brings rebirth; continue thought after thought to the end of life; rouse the mind and restrain oneself, day and night never ceasing” can be expressed as:
Single-mindedly recite the name; unbroken thought brings rebirth. Continue thought after thought to the end of life; rouse the mind and restrain oneself, day and night never ceasing.
These twenty-four
great characters
are the golden highroad to the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss
the program of practice of the Pure Land school, the wondrous method that ensures rebirth,
the very essence of Master Shandao’s Pure Land teaching. Those who practice thus
—of ten, ten are reborn; of a hundred, a hundred are reborn, forever enjoying unconditioned Dharma-bliss, and on to Buddhahood — how joyful!
On this, Master Yinguang instructed:

“The method of reciting the Buddha’s name is about four: recitation of the name, recitation before an image, recitation by visualization, and recitation of true reality. Among these four, only recitation of the name gathers the widest capacities, is the easiest to begin, and does not give rise to demonic obstructions.

Master Shandao said: ‘Sentient beings of the Dharma-ending age have floating consciousness, coarse minds and subtle realms, so visualization is hard to accomplish. Therefore the Great Sage in compassion
especially urged
exclusive recitation of the name
because recitation of the name is easy,
unbroken thought brings rebirth
’ I truly fear that some may not apply their minds well and so fall into a demonic state.”
(from the Collected Essays of Master Yinguang
Reply to Layman Wu Xizhen, First Letter)
Continue thought after thought to the end of life; rouse the mind, restrain oneself, day and night never ceasing
” — this is the key to the accomplishment of name-recitation, and we must unfailingly follow it. All study and all teaching likewise should revolve around this core, so as to ensure rebirth.

Conversely, if one recitates “without a mind of thought-after-thought continuity, and with a will to break off again and again,” relying upon this negligent practice, then to hope for rebirth at the final hour is difficult — for the present is the cause and the final hour the fruit. This is [spoken by] the manifestation of Amitabha Buddha
Master Yongming instructed:
“If speech and conduct do not match
(if what one says and what one does are not in accord)
, with weak strength of faith, without a mind of thought-after-thought continuity, and a will to break off again and again
(the mindful thought of recitation broken off by deluded thoughts)
relying
(trusting in)
this negligence, then at the final hour, hoping for rebirth, he is but obstructed by karmic hindrances, and in fear will be unable to meet his good friend
(for fear he will not meet a spiritual friend who can arouse his right mindfulness at death)
; the winds and fire press upon him, and right mindfulness is not accomplished. Why is this? For
the present is the cause and the final hour is the fruit

; so the cause must be real, and the fruit will then not be empty. If one wishes the ten thoughts at death to be accomplished, he should but prepare the ferry and the bridge in advance, gather together merit, and dedicate it to that hour, so that thought after thought is without lapse — then there is nothing to fear.”
(from the Collected Essays on the Common Return of All Good Deeds)
[The ten thoughts at the moment of death accomplished] Accomplishing the ten unbroken thoughts at the moment of death.
(See further
“The Ten Thoughts at Death: Unbroken Thought Brings Rebirth”
, in that article.)
[Preparing the ferry and the bridge] “Ferry and bridge”: a crossing and a bridge, that is, making preparation in advance.
Question: How can one accomplish “unbroken thought brings rebirth”?
Answer: Master Shandao instructed:
“May all people reflect well within themselves: whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, one must
rouse the mind, restrain oneself, day and night never ceasing
. When the final thought ends life, the next thought forthwith brings rebirth; forever enjoying unconditioned Dharma-bliss, and on to Buddhahood — how joyful!”
In this instruction,
the six characters “rouse the mind, restrain oneself, day and night never ceasing”

are the essential secret of accomplishing “unbroken thought brings rebirth,” making thought-after-thought continuing a firmly formed habit. Thus, at the moment of death, one is able to keep thought after thought unbroken and be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss. To this end, one must certainly firm up one’s resolve for the Way and, with tireless diligence, accomplish “rouse the mind, restrain oneself, day and night never ceasing.” In today’s world, the sea of desire runs wild, people’s minds turn toward evil, and they are the more off the Way. Adding to this, false teachers fan the flames and invert the teaching, so that reciters of the Buddha’s name are immersed in an evil cauldron without precedent in history. To firm up one’s resolve for the Way and remain unstained by the mud, I advise you to take up the Sutra of the Buddha’s Bequeathed Teaching (see further
“Commentary on the Sutra of the Buddha’s Bequeathed Teaching”

), recite it often and practice it, so as to withstand the disturbances from within and without and the invasions of material desire, and accomplish the work of the Way. As for the specific method of recitation, see
“Mindful Recitation”
. As long as you are earnest, diligent, hardworking, and persevering, you will certainly accomplish “unbroken thought brings rebirth.”
Question: How does one accomplish
“continue thought after thought
to the end of life”?
Answer:
The Avatamsaka Sutra says:
“Never forget the first resolve, and only then is the end attained.”
This means: never forget the original resolve, and only then can one carry through from beginning to end (persevere to the very end). That is,
never forgetting the original resolve, one can overcome all difficulties and, unbending, walk from the starting point to the goal. Hence the Avatamsaka Sutra also says:
“All the Tathagatas of the three times
(without exception)
protect and keep in mind the first resolve.”

For one who recites the Buddha’s name, one must always remember the original resolve to practice Buddhism so as to put an end to birth and death, and with unshakable perseverance, overcoming all difficulties, tirelessly accomplish “continue thought after thought to the end of life.”

When Buddhist practitioners first resolve to practice, they are all vigorous and diligent, advancing in both understanding and practice. But as time passes, some cannot bear the refining of practice and gradually lose the advancing mind of the Way they once had, becoming lax and indulgent; others simply give up, drifting with the world, and even falling into the trap of fame and profit. Facing the difficulty of practice, it is often said in the Buddhist community: “The first year a renunciant, the Buddha is in his heart; the second year, the Buddha is before his eyes; the third year, the Buddha is far off in the sky.” So those who practice Buddhism must
not forget the original resolve
and be as at the very first
, so as to accomplish the work of the Way.

Master Xuanzang’s journey to India to fetch the scriptures set a shining example of “never forget the first resolve, and only then is the end attained.” The Master left home at thirteen in the Jingtu Monastery at Luoyang, and thereafter traveled to various places, seeking out noted teachers. In the course of listening to the teachings, he was deeply troubled that the various explanations were in conflict and that he could find no resolution. In order to seek the true Dharma and set things in order at their source, he made the vow to travel west. In the first year of the Zhenguan era (
), when his request to the court for permission to travel west came to nothing, the Master set out privately from Chang’an with his fellow practitioners to seek the scriptures in the west.

The Master’s company first passed through Lanzhou and reached Liangzhou (Wuwei, Gansu). To avoid being questioned and searched along the way, they traveled by night and lay hidden by day. Then, passing through the Jade Gate Pass, crossing the Fiery Mountain, traversing thousands of li of the vast shifting sands, going through the uninhabited lands where vipers and wolves prowl, having tasted every hardship, they at last reached Yi-wu (Hami, Xinjiang). After a brief rest, the company pressed on and arrived at the kingdom of Gaochang (Turpan, Xinjiang). Then, crossing the Congling range and the Iron Gate, they reached the kingdom of Baktria (in the north of present-day Afghanistan), passed through the kingdom of Udyana (the Swat region of Pakistan), and arrived at the kingdom of Kashmir (northwestern India). After studying there for two years, Master Xuanzang pressed on again and, in the fifth year of the Zhenguan era (

), arrived at Nalanda monastery in the kingdom of Magadha, where he studied under Master Silabhadra, learning the doctrine of Consciousness-Only. Master Xuanzang studied at Nalanda for thirteen years, studying the scriptures and treatises of both the Greater and Lesser Vehicles, and gained the very essence of the Dharma.

In order to fulfill the original resolve he had made, Master Xuanzang, though he endured a thousand hardships and ten thousand difficulties on the road, and sometimes even peril to his life, never once retreated a half step. In particular, when crossing the great desert of the Mobei Sands between Lop Nur and the Jade Gate Pass, he encountered unimaginable difficulties. The Master’s biography describes it: “Above, no birds in flight; below, no roaming beasts; grass and trees do not grow, and the tracks of men are utterly rare; at times the wind rolls up sand and stones, at times the sun blazes down and the heat steams; at times he sees withered bones covering the plain, the remnants of battlefields; at times he sees fierce beasts and phantom shapes

By day, under the blazing sun, the temperature of the desert was extreme, and there was no place to set foot. The Master had no recourse but to bury himself in the sand and wait for night to continue his journey. In the boundless desert, the Master also once lost his way. Under such desperate circumstances, some of the company, unable to bear it, gave up the westward journey, and others died along the way. Master Xuanzang, never forgetting his original resolve, holding to the determination “I would rather take one step toward the West and die, than take half a step toward the East and live,” enduring hunger and thirst, his life hanging by a thread, at last reached Nalanda monastery in India, gained the very essence of the Dharma, and fully fulfilled his great vow to go west and seek the scriptures.
I would rather take one step toward the West and die, than take half a step toward the East and live.
In
concrete practice, Master Yinguang instructed:

“Whether at home or in a monastery, one must respect superiors and be kind to those below. Endure what others cannot endure; practice what others cannot practice. Take on others’ burdens and bring about others’ good. When sitting quietly, always reflect on one’s own faults; in idle conversation, never discuss others’ wrongs.

Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, whether dressing or eating, from morning to evening, from evening to morning, let a single phrase of the Buddha’s name not be interrupted. Recite in a low voice, or recite silently; apart from recitation, do not give rise to any other thought. If a deluded thought should arise, put an end to it on the spot.

Always give rise to a mind of shame and repentance. Even if you have cultivations, always feel that your own effort is shallow, and never boast. Look only after your own affairs, not those of others. Look only at good examples, not at bad ones. Regard all people as bodhisattvas, and think that I alone am truly an ordinary being. If you can truly practice according to what I have said, you will certainly be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss.”
(from the Collected Essays of Master Yinguang, Third Compilation
Reply to Layman Ye Fubei, First Letter)

Furthermore, you may also adopt the method of reciting the Buddha’s name in accord with the breath, so as to form it into a habit, which makes it easier to accomplish “continue thought after thought to the end of life.” (See further
“Essentials of Breathing Recitation”
, in that article.)
